guideTitle: Best Electric Kettles With Tea Infusers (2026)
metaTitle: Best Electric Kettles With Tea Infusers (2026)
metaDescription: Six electric kettles with built-in tea infusers, compared on temperature control, glass versus stainless bodies, infuser design and how easy each is to clean.
expertTake: The Cosori 1.7 liter with infuser is the pick because it combines a plastic-free water path, six presets and a long keep-warm hold in a body that is easy to clean. The Chefman 1.2 liter glass kettle is the value pick for one or two cups of loose leaf. Anyone who drinks bagged tea only should skip the infuser feature and buy a plain boiler.
introParagraphs: A kettle with a built-in infuser lets you heat and steep in one vessel, which saves a teapot and a step. The idea is simple, but the execution varies: some baskets sit loosely and leak leaves, some trap scale and some are awkward to lift out hot.

We focused on how each basket is built, how the kettle holds temperature while the tea steeps, and how easy it is to clean afterward. Leaf tea leaves oils and tannins behind, so cleanup design matters as much as the heating spec.

products.name: Cosori 1.7L Kettle with Tea Infuser and 6 Presets
products.description:
Cosori builds this kettle around a thermostat that holds six temperatures from 165 degrees F up to a full boil, and adds a removable infuser for steeping loose leaf inside the vessel. A one hour keep-warm hold lets the tea steep at a steady temperature instead of cooling during the brew. Every water-contact surface is listed as plastic free, so a long steep does not pick up a resin taste.

The limit here is that a 1.7 liter body is large for a single mug, and a loose infuser basket still lets fine leaves slip through on a vigorous pour. Next to the Chefman 1.2 liter, the Cosori holds nearly half again more water and gives far finer temperature control, but the Chefman's glass lets you watch the color develop.

In year three the infuser is the wear part. Rinse tea oils out of the mesh each time and the stainless interior stays clean for years. Descale the element on a monthly schedule in hard water, and keep the lid hinge dry, since that is where plastic trim sits.
products.bestFor: Loose leaf drinkers who brew different teas at different temperatures.
pros: Six presets starting at 165 degrees F
Sixty minute keep-warm supports long steeps
Plastic-free water path keeps taste clean
Large 1.7 liter body for a pot of tea
cons: Fine leaves can slip past the basket
Too large for a single mug

products.name: Chefman 1.2L Glass Kettle with Stainless Infuser
products.description:
This Chefman is the straightforward infuser kettle: a 1.2 liter glass body, a 1500 watt element and a stainless removable basket. Blue LEDs show when the water is heating, which makes the glass part of the display. It heats to a full boil only, so it is aimed at black, herbal and fruit teas.

The cost of simplicity is control. With no temperature setting, delicate green tea needs a manual wait after the boil, and compared with the Cosori you lose keep-warm and precision. Glass also chips and shows scale, so a hard knock matters more than on stainless.

A stainless basket is easier to clean than a plastic one and does not stain from strong tea. Rinse it after each brew and descale monthly so the glass stays clear. For one or two cups of loose leaf per day, this kettle does the job at the lowest complexity of the six. If you do want green tea from it, boil, lift the lid and wait about two minutes before adding the basket, which brings the water close to 175 degrees F without any electronics.
products.bestFor: One or two mugs of black or herbal loose leaf tea.
pros: 1500W element boils a small fill quickly
Stainless basket resists staining
Glass body shows the brew developing
Simple to operate with no menus
cons: Glass can chip or show scale

products.name: Chefman Temperature Control Glass Kettle with Infuser
products.description:
This model adds preset temperatures to the Chefman glass-and-infuser formula. Tri-color LEDs signal standby, heating and ready, and the presets run from 160 up to a full boil. The infuser rides inside the glass vessel so you can see the leaves open.

The tradeoff is glass fragility and a smaller selection of finer steps than the Cosori. Beside the 1.2 liter Chefman, it costs more complexity for the ability to steep green tea correctly, which many buyers value.

Upkeep follows the glass rule: wipe and descale on schedule, and rinse the infuser after tea oils have time to dry. Expect a good compromise for someone who wants to watch leaves unfurl and still hit the right temperature.
products.bestFor: Green and white tea drinkers who like watching the leaves.
pros: Presets begin at 160 degrees F
Glass shows leaves unfurling
LED colors show each state clearly
Removable infuser for loose leaf

products.name: INTASTING 1L Borosilicate Kettle with Infuser
products.description:
INTASTING advertises temperature accuracy within one degree F, which is tighter than the five-degree class of most rivals. The vessel is borosilicate glass, which tolerates thermal swings better than ordinary glass, and a keep-warm hold lasts up to an hour. The infuser sits inside for steeping.

The tradeoff is capacity and cost. At one liter it fills four cups, so a family pot needs a second round. Against the Narcissus at 1.8 liters, it gives up volume for finer control, which matters for delicate teas more than for big batches.

For maintenance, borosilicate resists cracking from a hot refill, but scale still shows and needs regular clearing. Rinse the infuser mesh promptly. It suits a careful tea drinker brewing a single pot at a time. Pre-warm the infuser by rinsing it with hot water before loading leaves, and keep the lid closed during the steep so the stated one degree accuracy is not undone by heat escaping.
products.bestFor: Careful brewers who need tight temperature accuracy.
pros: Advertised accuracy within one degree F
Borosilicate glass tolerates thermal swings
Keep-warm holds up to an hour
Removable infuser inside the vessel
cons: One liter fills only about four cups

products.name: Narcissus 1.8L Kettle with Removable Infuser
products.description:
Narcissus offers the biggest body here, 1.8 liters, with a 1200 watt element and temperature control within five degrees F. A removable mesh infuser handles loose leaf. The size lets it steep a full pot for a group.

The tradeoff is speed and precision. A 1200 watt element needs longer than a 1500 watt one to heat a large fill, and the five-degree accuracy is looser than the INTASTING. Versus the Chefman Custom-Temp at the same 1.8 liter size, it has a slightly lower power rating.

Expect to descale on schedule since a big vessel holds a lot of hard water. The mesh basket needs rinsing after each use. It makes sense for a household or office that serves tea to several people.
products.bestFor: Tea service for several people at once.
pros: 1.8 liter body serves a group
Temperature control within five degrees F
Removable mesh infuser included
Large capacity reduces refills
cons: 1200W is slower for a full fill

products.name: Chefman Custom-Temp 1.8L Stainless Kettle with Infuser
products.description:
Chefman's Custom-Temp kettle puts a stainless body around the infuser idea. Color-coded LEDs show the heating state, a Keep Hot mode avoids reheating between cups, and the infuser is removable. The listing frames it as faster than a stovetop kettle.

The tradeoff against the glass models is that you cannot see the leaves or the water through the walls. Compared with the Narcissus at the same size, it is sturdier and does not chip, but it hides scale and tea stains inside.

For ownership, stainless wipes clean and shrugs off knocks. Rinse the infuser and descale on schedule, and it should outlast the glass kettles on this list. It is the durable choice for a busy kitchen. Because you cannot see inside, get in the habit of peeking at the water level markings before each boil, and wipe the inside with a soft cloth every few weeks to catch any tannin ring before it sets into a permanent stain.
products.bestFor: Busy kitchens that want a tough body and a big pot.
pros: Stainless body resists chips and knocks
Keep Hot mode avoids reheating
1.8 liter capacity for a full pot
Removable infuser for loose leaf
cons: Opaque body hides water and scale

buyingCriteria.explanation: A good basket has fine enough mesh to hold small leaves, a handle you can lift hot and a secure seat so it does not float. The Cosori and Chefman baskets are removable, which means you can empty them without dumping the kettle. Mesh that is too coarse lets fines into the cup, and a cramped basket stops leaves from unfurling. Judge by leaf size: whole leaf oolong needs room, broken black tea needs fine mesh. Leaves need room to swell, often to three times their dry volume, so a basket that is half the height of the vessel works better than a tiny tube. Also check that the basket can be lifted by a heat-safe handle, because pulling a steaming basket out with fingers is the most common minor burn.

Green and white tea scorch at a full boil, so a kettle that holds 165 to 175 degrees F improves flavor. The Cosori starts at 165 degrees F, the Chefman temperature model at 160, and the Chefman 1.2 liter only boils. If you drink black or herbal tea, a boil-only kettle is fine. Check the lowest preset, since that is the one delicate teas use. As a rule of thumb, green tea likes 160 to 175 degrees F, white tea about 175 to 185, oolong 185 to 205 and black tea near boiling. A kettle that skips the 175 range, as the Chefman 1.2 liter does, cannot make the best green tea without a manual wait.

Leaf tea steeps for two to five minutes, and the water cools during that time unless the kettle holds it. The Cosori's hour hold and the INTASTING's hour hold keep the temperature steady. A kettle without hold, like the Chefman 1.2 liter, loses a few degrees while you wait. For a long oolong steep, the hold is worth having.

Glass shows color and level but chips and shows scale. Stainless hides both and survives knocks. The INTASTING uses borosilicate glass, which handles thermal swings better than soda glass. If tea staining bothers you, remember that dark tannin films are more visible on glass, while on stainless they are hidden but still there.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Capacity for the way you brew
buyingCriteria.explanation: One liter fills four cups and 1.8 liters nearly seven. The INTASTING suits one person with a pot, and the Narcissus or Chefman Custom-Temp suit a group. Buyers often choose the largest body and then steep a single mug, and a high minimum fill line makes that wasteful.

Tea leaves oils and tannins, and loose leaf adds fines that settle at the bottom. A wide opening and a removable basket make cleanup quick. Narrow glass kettles need a brush. Rinse the basket right away, since dried tea oil is much harder to remove.

specDecoder.meaning: The advertised tolerance of the thermostat around the target. Plus or minus one degree is tighter than plus or minus five.
specDecoder.watchFor: The INTASTING lists one degree and the Narcissus lists five.

specDecoder.meaning: The coolest temperature the kettle will hold. It decides whether green and white tea can be brewed correctly.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Cosori starts at 165 degrees F and the Chefman temperature model at 160.

specDecoder.meaning: How long the kettle maintains the set temperature after heating. It matters for steeping and sipping.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Cosori and INTASTING list about an hour, and the Chefman 1.2 liter has none.

specDecoder.meaning: Glass with low thermal expansion, so hot water does not crack it as easily. It is not unbreakable.
specDecoder.watchFor: The INTASTING uses it, but treat any glass body gently.

specDecoder.meaning: Heating power in watts. Higher power heats a volume faster.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Narcissus and INTASTING use 1200W, below the 1500W Chefman 1.2 liter.

howWeEvaluated.title: Infuser practicality
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed basket size, mesh, removability and how it seats in the vessel. The Cosori and Chefman stainless basket rank well for ease. Coarse or cramped baskets score lower.

howWeEvaluated.title: Temperature handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared lowest preset and stated accuracy, from the INTASTING's one degree to the Narcissus's five. Finer control scores higher for delicate tea. We note these are listing specs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Hold performance
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at keep-warm length, since steeping needs steady heat. The Cosori and INTASTING hold about an hour. The Chefman 1.2 liter has none and scores lower here.

howWeEvaluated.title: Body and durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated stainless, glass and borosilicate. Stainless survives knocks, and glass shows the brew. Owner feedback patterns on chips and scale informed ranks.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleaning after tea
howWeEvaluated.description: We scored opening width and basket removal. Wide stainless bodies are the easiest to clean. Narrow glass bodies need extra care.

rows: Infuser and glass at entry price

cards.label: Glass
cards.text: The Chefman glass kettles and the INTASTING show the leaves and the water level. They chip and show scale and tannin film.

cards.label: Stainless
cards.text: The Cosori and Chefman Custom-Temp survive knocks and hide scale. You cannot watch the brew.

howToChoose.note: Choose glass for watching the steep; choose stainless for daily durability.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A removable fine-mesh basket, a low preset for delicate leaves and a keep-warm hold so the temperature stays steady during the steep.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Cosori 1.7 liter with infuser meets all three, and the INTASTING adds finer accuracy for a smaller pot.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You drink green or white tea daily and want presets and a plastic-free path, as on the Cosori 1.7 liter.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You steep black or herbal tea, where the Chefman 1.2 liter does the job.

maintenance.why: Tea oils dry into a film that is hard to remove. A quick rinse keeps mesh clear.
Scale on the element slows heating and clouds glass. Citric acid per directions clears it.
Dark rings form where tea sits. A paste of baking soda lifts them without scratching.
Damp hinges collect residue and can crack. Leave the lid open to air dry.
Spills at the base interrupt power. Wipe them dry.

faq.q: Is a kettle with an infuser better than a teapot?
faq.a: It saves a step and a dish, but it ties the brew to the heating vessel. A separate teapot lets the kettle boil the next batch while one steeps. The Cosori 1.7 liter is the best of this group for combined use.

faq.q: Can I use the infuser at a full boil?
faq.a: Yes for black and herbal tea, but delicate green and white teas turn bitter at that heat. Choose a model with presets from 160 to 175 degrees F for those leaves. The Chefman temperature model and Cosori cover that range.

faq.q: How long does a glass kettle last?
faq.a: With gentle handling it lasts years, but knocks and sudden temperature swings can crack it. Borosilicate, as on the INTASTING, handles swings better. Stainless models outlast both.
A stainless basket is neutral, but old tea oil left in mesh adds a stale note. Rinse after each use. Plastic baskets can retain flavor longer.

faq.q: Why do some leaves escape the basket?
faq.a: Mesh size is the cause. Fine fannings pass through coarse mesh, while whole leaf stays put. Match the mesh to your tea, or add a paper filter for very fine leaf.

faq.q: Does a bigger kettle make better tea?
faq.a: No. A big vessel only helps for groups. For one person, a smaller body heats faster and wastes less water. The INTASTING and Chefman 1.2 liter suit small servings.
